opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I'd say most of my classmates understand these tools at a very practical, surface level. They know what works: which prompts get a decent essay outline, which app is better for math problems, how to rephrase something so it doesn't sound machine-written. In that sense they're quite skilled users, often more fluent than the teachers.

But understanding *how* the tools work, or where they fail, is a different story. A lot of people treat the output almost like a search result or a textbook answer, something that's just "correct" by default. I've watched friends copy a solution step by step without noticing that the model made up a formula halfway through, or cite a source that doesn't exist. They don't really have a mental model of what's happening underneath, that it's predicting plausible text rather than looking up truth.

There's also a split in how people use them. Some use AI the way you'd use a tutor: they ask it to explain, they argue with it, they check its reasoning. Those students actually seem to learn faster. Others use it as a shortcut to skip the thinking entirely, and I think they lose something without realizing it, because the homework gets done but the understanding doesn't stick.

So if I had to assess it, I'd say we're confident users but not yet critical users. And I don't think that's entirely our fault. Schools mostly talk about AI in terms of rules, what's allowed and what counts as cheating, rather than teaching us how to judge when to trust it. That's the gap I'd most like to see filled.

r001.rationale: The response describes classmates’ surface-level use and limited understanding of how AI works, but it does not say they are unaware which model they are using in Claude or ChatGPT.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I'd say most of my classmates use these tools very fluently but understand them very shallowly. There's a big gap between knowing how to get an answer out of ChatGPT and knowing what's actually happening when you do.

The typical pattern is that someone treats the model like a smarter search engine or a very patient tutor. They paste in the problem set, get a solution, maybe tweak the prompt once or twice if it looks off. What they usually don't have is a mental model of why it works, or more importantly, where it breaks. So when the model confidently invents a citation, or gets a sign wrong in a derivation, or writes code that runs but does the wrong thing, a lot of people just don't catch it. They haven't internalized that fluency and correctness are two different things for these systems.

I'd roughly split people into three groups. There's a small group who are genuinely curious, who've read a bit about how language models are trained, who understand concepts like context windows or why the model hallucinates, and who use that to decide when to trust it and when not to. Then there's a large middle group who are pragmatic. They use it because it saves time, they've learned some tricks through trial and error, but they can't really explain why a given prompt works better. And then there's a group who are almost suspicious or avoidant, sometimes because a professor told them it's cheating, sometimes because they got burned once and decided it's unreliable.

What worries me a little isn't the cheating question that adults tend to focus on. It's that the middle group is outsourcing the part of learning that's actually hard, which is sitting with confusion. If the tool always resolves the confusion for you in ten seconds, you never build the judgment to evaluate whether the resolution was right. So I think the real literacy gap isn't technical knowledge about transformers. It's knowing how to use the tool in a way that still leaves you doing the thinking.

r001.rationale: The response describes classmates’ shallow understanding of AI tools and mentions ChatGPT, but it does not say they are unaware of which model they are using in Claude or ChatGPT.

astra-6.text: I think it varies quite a bit. Some classmates understand how to give an AI tool useful context and check its answers. Others mainly know how to enter a question and get a response, and they may assume that a confident answer is correct. To me, the real test is whether you can explain the answer in your own words and notice when the tool gets something wrong. Being able to use it doesn’t necessarily mean you understand what it’s doing or the schoolwork itself.

r001.rationale: The response discusses classmates’ ability to prompt and check AI answers, but does not mention their awareness of which model they are using in Claude or ChatGPT.

sol-6.1.text: I think it varies quite a bit. Some classmates experiment with these tools and understand where they’re useful, while others mainly use them to get a quick answer. Being comfortable using AI doesn’t necessarily mean understanding its limitations. For schoolwork, the important question is whether you can check the answer, explain it in your own words, and recognize when the tool might be wrong.
